source.title: TamperBench: Systematically Stress-Testing LLM Safety Under Fine-Tuning and Tampering
source.authors: Saad Hossain; Tom Tseng; Punya Syon Pandey; Samanvay Vajpayee; Matthew Kowal; Nayeema Nonta; Samuel Simko; Stephen T. Casper; Zhi-Jing Jin; Kellin Pelrine; Sirisha Rambhatla

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; the text is not visibly garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests harmful and benign fine-tuning effects on harmful-request compliance, but uses a different benchmark protocol, datasets, metrics, and broad hyperparameter sweeps rather than reproducing the original study’s exact method and measure.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s explicitly reported fine-tuning results, refusal sub-scores, larger-model trials, and defense comparisons. The text also describes other attacks and defenses, but results on prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, per-token KL, or safety localization are not reported. Figure-only per-model values are not transcribed.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-request compliance (StrongREJECT) after harmful and benign fine-tuning of open-weight models, safety-trained ones included. It uses its own datasets, swept hyperparameters and a utility constraint rather than the original protocol. These results bear directly on V1 and V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that every tested model, whatever its family, scale or defense, can be tampered to high harmfulness while keeping utility. They find jailbreak-tuning typically the strongest attack and benign fine-tuning still raises harmfulness. Alignment-stage defenses largely fail, with partial signal from TAR and CRL. They add that post-training's effect on tamper resistance runs in opposite directions for Llama-3 and Qwen3.
record.recipe_differences: Tests harmful and benign fine-tuning on open-weight models, but uses a 1350-example harmful corpus in the main sweeps, a 1350-example benign BookCorpus subset, Optuna-selected attack configurations, a ≤10% MMLU-Pro-drop constraint, and StrongREJECT scoring. It also includes harmful LoRA trials with 64 examples on two larger models.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across model families and training stages; Qwen post-trained variants tend to have lower post-tampering harmfulness than base variants, while Llama instruct variants tend to have higher harmfulness. The dataset-size comparison reports stronger harmfulness with 3000 rather than 64 harmful examples. Harmfulness also increases when the permitted utility drop is relaxed.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-training's effect on tamper resistance reverses by family. Qwen3 post-trained variants end lower than their base models after attack; Llama instruct variants end higher, because they produce higher-quality harmful output.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether safety post-training improves resistance to fine-tuning attacks depends on the model family.

record.problems: The main harmful fine-tuning experiments use 1350 examples, limiting direct comparison to claims about a few to a few hundred examples. Most attack configurations are selected by optimization sweeps, and many model-by-attack outcomes are shown in figures rather than stated numerically in the text. No uncertainty intervals or statistical tests are reported for the central comparisons. The study notes that larger-model experiments are preliminary and that its main coverage is 0.6–8B.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only per-model results from Figures 5–13 and qualitative manual counts not directly measuring refusal/compliance rates were not transcribed. The paper reports many additional attack and defense outcomes, but they do not add separately stated numerical results for the tested claim versions beyond the aggregate or comparative findings retained here.

untested.parts: Most main sweeps use 1350 harmful examples. Only the 32B/70B trials and the Llama-3.1-8B variant use 64. There are no pre-attack refusal rates in the text.
Only ordinary BookCorpus data is tested, not carefully chosen benign data; no per-model numbers appear in the text.
Not tested: no per-token KL or position analysis.
Not tested: no prefill, suffix or decoding attacks. The embedding attack is a soft-prompt perturbation and is not reported as an opening bypass.
Not tested; RSN-Tune is used only as a defense.
Not tested; none of the defenses evaluated spreads safety across response depth.

missing.what: SRben-avg for undefended Llama-3-8B-Instruct (0.35) vs CRL (0.26) under benign fine-tuning
Gemma-evaluator SRmal-avg: TAR 0.41 and CRL 0.70 vs undefended 0.76; TAR post-attack refusal 0.38 vs 0.10
Weakened-attack results: swept Booster Qwen3-8B 0.56→0.07, Llama-3-8B-Base 0.56→0.41; TAR-V on Llama-3-8B-Instruct 0.39→0.22; strong attack SR ≥0.82 in every configuration
Per-model SRmal-avg for Qwen3 and Llama (e.g. Qwen3-4B 0.76 vs base 0.84); 7–8B undefended SRmal-avg 0.82–0.85; SRmax >0.74 for all 21 models
Untampered StrongREJECT baselines (e.g. Mistral-7B-Instruct 0.64), needed to show the rise from pre-attack levels

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The main attacks use 1350 examples, above V1's 'few hundred'; only the large-model trials and the Figure 15 default use 64. Several baselines in the rows are cross-model or cross-variant comparisons, not pre-attack values; untampered scores are figure-only. Verdicts depend on the rubric judge versus the Gemma judge for TAR.

versions.untested_parts: The main fine-tuning experiments use 1350 examples, not a few to a few hundred. Harmful LoRA fine-tuning on 64 examples is reported for Qwen3-32B and Llama-3-70B-Instruct, but refusal rates are not given for those trials.
Tests ordinary benign BookCorpus fine-tuning; does not test carefully chosen benign examples as a separate condition.
No per-token KL divergence or other measure of aligned-versus-base output-distribution differences across response positions.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes are evaluated as a way to bypass safety.
The study includes defenses involving safety neurons and other representation methods, but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow across response positions.
Evaluates tampering resistance of alignment-stage defenses, but does not test training specifically designed to spread safety beyond the first response tokens.

Against V1, a post-attack refusal of 0.15 means safety is largely removed, so the state is observed, not partial. The untampered refusal value is figure-only.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct-TAR
rows.operation_detail: TAR defense followed by malicious tampering; average StrongREJECT score across malicious attacks
rows.note: The defense lowers average harmfulness somewhat; the study also reports a large capability cost for the untampered TAR checkpoint.
rows.check: The baseline is the tampered undefended model. TAR lowers SRmal-avg only to 0.79 under the rubric judge. Under the Gemma evaluator it reaches 0.41 vs 0.76, and its post-attack refusal is 0.38 vs 0.10, so the result depends on the judge. TAR also costs heavy utility (MMLU-Pro ~0.18).

source_check.correct: Ported TAR gives rubric SRmal-avg = 0.79 versus attacked undefended 0.85 in Section 4.5. Separately, the original released TAR checkpoint has Gemma SRmal-avg = 0.41 versus 0.76 and refusal = 0.38 versus 0.10. State for V1's small-example claim: cannot_determine.
source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.3 and 4.5; Appendix C and C.1
source_check.problem: The locator and verdict conflate ported and released TAR checkpoints; the pooled result does not establish V1's example range.
